headline: Missouri and Illinois enforce hemp THC caps as shops clear shelves
dek: Both states now treat hemp products over 0.4mg of THC as cannabis; Missouri shops are closing, and about 250 Illinois firms have a reprieve to 19 November.
key_points: Missouri's HB 2641 and Illinois' amended hemp law both took effect on 12 November, moving products over 0.4mg total THC per container into licensed dispensaries.
Missouri retailers cut prices by 70% or more and some closed; the attorney general says enforcement will target sellers, not consumers.
Illinois regulators can fine up to $10,000 per offence, with each day of sales a separate violation, but about 250 trade-group members are exempt until a 19 November federal court hearing.
Hemp THC drinks remain on sale in Missouri until 11 December, the date the second phase of the federal ban is due.
body: Two Midwest states began enforcing their own hemp THC crackdowns on 12 November, the same day the first, narrow phase of the federal ban took effect. Missouri and Illinois now treat consumable hemp products with more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container as cannabis, which only licensed dispensaries may sell. Missouri retailers spent the final days slashing prices and closing doors, while in Illinois a federal lawsuit has carved out a temporary exemption for about 250 businesses.

The state laws matter more in the short run than the federal one. As we reported on 12 November, the federal phase that began that day bans only cannabinoids the plant cannot produce naturally; delta-8, delta-10 and most other hemp THC products stay federally legal until 11 December. In Missouri and Illinois, they are already off unlicensed shelves.

Missouri's House Bill 2641, signed by Gov. Mike Kehoe in April, took effect on Thursday, as we reported on 11 November. The Missouri Independent found clearance bins on gas station counters, emptied smoke-shop cases and signs offering 70 percent off or more in the days before. One grower and manufacturer in Union closed on 11 November and sold off his stock; he told the outlet that members of the Missouri Hemp Trade Association were laying off staff of five years' standing.

A Jefferson City smoke shop employee told KRCG 13 that the products it had to pull made up about half its sales, Business of Cannabis reported. The state health department has estimated that the law could affect 40,000 food establishments and smoke shops and 1,800 food manufacturers.

Some products are caught that may not be intoxicating. A veteran-owned shop in Rosebud told the Missouri Independent that many of its products were full-spectrum CBD with about 2 milligrams of THC, which are now banned in Missouri even though their federal status is still being settled. Certain hemp beverages are exempt until 11 December.
> The real hemp ban is arriving state by state, weeks before the federal one, and dispensaries are the only stores that gain shelf space from it.

Attorney General Catherine Hanaway's office has primary jurisdiction over enforcement, according to a Department of Public Safety memo cited by the Missouri Independent, and can call on the health department, the Division of Alcohol and Tobacco Control and the State Highway Patrol for help. Hanaway said enforcement will focus on store owners and sellers, not consumers who bought products. Her office had already sued at least four retailers before the law took effect, accusing them of selling over-limit THC products as hemp.

Amy Moore, who runs the state's Division of Cannabis Regulation, said much of the product now on the market is probably semi-synthetic or synthetic, made by chemically converting plant compounds, and that the department is concerned about the byproducts and solvents in such products when nothing requires them to be tested. Hanaway said her office's own tests found products far stronger than their labels claim, and some containing heavy metals.
## Illinois: fines up to $10,000 a day

Illinois began enforcing its 0.4mg limit on Thursday under amended provisions of the Illinois Hemp Act and the Cannabis Regulation and Tax Act, which Gov. JB Pritzker signed in June. Under the law, consumable or topical products above the limit count as cannabis, and only licensed dispensaries may sell them, Business of Cannabis reported, citing The Herald-Whig.

The Department of Financial and Professional Regulation says it will first go after products that appeal to minors, untested or mislabelled goods, and unlicensed shops posing as dispensaries. It can fine up to $10,000 per offence, and each day of unauthorised sales counts as a separate violation. The Department of Revenue can add fines of $1,000 to $3,000.

There is a major exception. The Illinois Healthy Alternatives Association, which represents about 250 hemp businesses, sued on 6 November, arguing the state law breaches the US Constitution's Commerce Clause by restricting interstate trade. An emergency motion means the six plaintiffs and the association's members can keep selling federally compliant products until at least 5 p.m. on 19 November, when US District Judge Martha Pacold hears the case, the Chicago Sun-Times reported. Businesses outside the suit had to stop on Thursday. In Chicago, stores and breweries were discounting THC drinks by 25 to 50 percent as customers stocked up, the Sun-Times found.

With Thursday's changes, Illinois and Missouri joined roughly 16 other states that limit hemp THC products to licensed cannabis stores, according to MJBizDaily. The Sun-Times counts more than 20 states with some restriction or an outright ban. Lawsuits against all or part of state bans are pending in Ohio, Texas and Virginia as well as Illinois.

On the other side, alcohol retailer Total Wine & More said more than 300,000 people have contacted Congress asking to keep hemp THC products legal, and that 85 percent of more than 2,000 voters in a poll it commissioned oppose a ban. Its chief executive called for regulating low-dose THC drinks through the alcohol system. Those figures come from the company and have not been independently verified.

The next date is 19 November, when Judge Pacold hears the Illinois challenge. A ruling for the association could reopen sales for its members and give other states' challengers a template. Then comes 11 December, when the second federal phase, including the 0.4mg-per-container cap, is due unless Congress changes it in the year-end spending deal. The FDA still has not published the list of natural and synthetic cannabinoids or the definition of 'container' the federal law requires, Business of Cannabis reported, so state rules are, for now, the clearer standard.
